questions.q: You approach an unmarked, equal intersection. A car approaches from your right. Who goes first?
questions.e: At an equal intersection with no signs or lights, right-before-left applies: traffic from the right goes first. Arrival order and speed are irrelevant.

questions.q: You reach a stop sign. The crossing road is clearly empty in both directions. What must you do?
a: Slow down and continue if clear
Come to a complete stop, then proceed
questions.e: The stop sign always requires a full stop — even when the road is visibly empty. Rolling through slowly is the classic exam trap.

questions.q: Shark's teeth (haaientanden) are painted across your lane at a crossing. What do they mean?
a: Give way to the crossing traffic
questions.e: Shark's teeth painted on the road carry the same authority as a give-way sign: you must give way to the traffic on the crossing road.

questions.q: What does this triangle-on-its-point sign require?
a: A complete stop in all cases
Give way to crossing traffic — stopping only if needed
Nothing — it is only a warning
questions.e: The give-way sign (B6) requires you to yield to traffic on the crossing road. Unlike the stop sign, you only stop if someone is actually coming.

questions.q: You are about to enter a roundabout with give-way markings at the entry. A car is already driving on the roundabout. Who goes first?
a: The car already on the roundabout
questions.e: With shark's teeth or give-way signs at the entries — the normal Dutch setup — traffic already on the roundabout has priority.

questions.q: You want to turn left at an intersection. An oncoming car continues straight ahead. Who goes first?
questions.e: Traffic going straight on the same road goes before traffic that is turning. Your left turn crosses the oncoming car's path, so it goes first.

questions.q: You are driving out of a private driveway (uitrit) onto the street. Who must you give way to?
a: Only cars coming from the right
questions.e: Leaving an exit or driveway puts you last in line: you yield to all other traffic, including cyclists and pedestrians on the pavement you cross.

questions.q: An ambulance approaches with blue flashing lights AND siren. What is the rule?
a: Only cars in its lane must react
All road users must let it pass
It must still wait at give-way signs
questions.e: An emergency vehicle using both blue lights and siren outranks everyone — all road users must make way. It sits at the very top of the priority ladder.

questions.q: The traffic light shows green, but a police officer at the intersection signals you to stop. What do you do?
questions.e: A police officer directing traffic overrides the traffic light, just as the light overrides the signs. Follow the officer.

questions.q: What does this sign tell you?
a: A general danger ahead — be alert
questions.e: A red triangle is always a warning, never a command. The exclamation mark is the general danger sign: something ahead the other symbols don't cover.

questions.q: What does the red disc with a white horizontal bar mean?
a: No entry — you may not drive in
questions.e: This is the no-entry sign — typically the exit of a one-way street. You may not drive past it in this direction.

questions.q: What does this plain red ring with an empty white centre mean?
a: Closed to traffic in both directions
questions.e: The empty red ring (C1) closes the road to traffic in both directions — nobody may drive through.

questions.q: What does this sign forbid?
questions.e: Red circle with two cars, the left one red: no overtaking. Red circles always mean 'may not' — the symbol tells you what.

questions.q: You face a blue circle with a white arrow curving right. May you continue straight ahead?
a: Yes, the arrow is only a suggestion
Only if no one is behind you
questions.e: A blue circle is a command (gebod). The arrow shows the only permitted direction — you must turn right.

questions.q: Which sign category does a blue SQUARE belong to?
questions.e: Blue square or rectangle = information: it neither forbids nor commands. Compare: blue circle = command, red circle = prohibition, red triangle = warning.

questions.q: A single solid centre line runs next to your lane. A slow tractor drives ahead and the road looks clear. May you cross the line to overtake?
a: No — a solid line may not be crossed
questions.e: A solid line is a wall: you may not cross it, however clear the road looks. Only a dashed line may be crossed when safe.

questions.q: Does this sign require you to give way to cyclists?
a: No — it warns that crossing cyclists are ahead
questions.e: A red triangle never requires an action — it warns. Whether you must yield at the crossing itself is decided by signs or shark's teeth there, not by this triangle.

questions.q: You pass this town-name sign. There is no speed sign anywhere. What is the limit?
questions.e: The town-name sign marks the start of the built-up area (bebouwde kom) — and with it the default limit of 50, no number needed.

questions.q: You pass the town-name sign with a red line through it. No other signs. How fast may you go?
questions.e: Leaving the built-up area, the default outside limit applies: 80 km/h. The road type sets the limit when no sign does.

questions.q: You are on the autosnelweg at two in the afternoon. No matrix boards are lit. Your maximum speed?
questions.e: Between 06:00 and 19:00 every Dutch motorway is capped at 100. The 130 on the entry signs applies only at night, and only where signed.

questions.q: It is 22:00 on the autosnelweg and this sign applies to your stretch. Your maximum?
questions.e: At night (19:00–06:00), 130 is allowed where signed. The 100 cap is a daytime rule (06:00–19:00).

questions.q: You entered past this zone sign, turned into a side street, and see no speed sign there. How fast may you go?
questions.e: A zone sign covers the whole area and is not repeated on side streets. It holds until you pass the grey end-of-zone sign.

questions.q: Outside the built-up area you pass this end-of-50 sign. What applies now?
questions.e: The end sign means the posted limit is over — you fall back to the default for the road type. Outside the built-up area that is 80.

questions.q: On a curve, this blue square shows 50 km/h. You drive 60. Is that an offence in itself?
a: No — it is an advisory speed, not a limit
questions.e: A blue square is information: this is the adviessnelheid, the recommended speed. Exceeding it is not an offence in itself — but the road's real limit and your duty to drive safely still stand.

questions.q: You drive into an area marked with this sign. What speed applies?
questions.e: This is the erf (woonerf): the street belongs to residents, children may play on it, and you drive at walking pace (stapvoets) — about 15 km/h in practice.

questions.q: Night, motorway signed 130, and you are towing a caravan. Your maximum?
questions.e: A car with a trailer or caravan may never exceed 90. Of all limits that apply — road, sign, vehicle — the lowest always wins.

questions.q: You turn right into a side street. A cyclist on the cycle path beside you continues straight. Who goes first?
a: Whoever is closer to the corner
questions.e: Traffic going straight on the same road goes before turning traffic — and the cycle path counts as the same road. Mirror, shoulder, cycle path, then turn.

questions.q: At a zebra crossing, a person is pushing their bicycle across. Must you give way?
a: Yes — pushing a bike makes them a pedestrian
Only if they raise a hand
questions.e: Someone walking with their bike is legally a pedestrian, and pedestrians on or clearly about to cross a zebra have priority.

questions.q: A cyclist RIDES across the zebra crossing in front of you. Do they have priority because of the zebra?
a: No — the zebra gives riders no priority
questions.e: The zebra protects walkers, not riders. A riding cyclist has no zebra priority — though you must still avoid endangering them.

questions.q: A moped with a BLUE number plate rides ahead of you in town. Where does it belong, and how fast may it go?
questions.e: Blue plate = snorfiets: limited to 25 km/h and it rides on the cycle path. Yellow plate = bromfiets: 45, and on the road in town.

questions.q: Inside the built-up area, where does a yellow-plate moped (bromfiets) ride?
a: On the road, with the cars
questions.e: Inside the built-up area the bromfiets rides on the carriageway with the cars — that has been its place since the nineties. Do not expect it to move to the cycle path.

questions.q: At an unmarked equal intersection, a tram approaches from your LEFT. Who goes first?
a: You — traffic from the left yields
questions.e: The tram beats right-before-left: at equal intersections a tram has priority from any direction. Rails override the compass.

questions.q: Inside the built-up area, a bus at a bus stop signals that it wants to pull out. What must you do?
a: Give it the opportunity to pull out
questions.e: In the built-up area you must give a bus the chance to leave its stop when it signals. A small but real priority for the bus.

questions.q: At a red light a truck waits, indicating right. There is space to ride up along its right side to the stop line. Do you take it?
questions.e: That space is the heart of the dode hoek — the driver cannot see you, and his right turn sweeps exactly through it. Stay behind, visible in his mirrors.

questions.q: What is the blood alcohol limit for a driver in the first five years of holding a licence?
questions.e: Novice drivers — the first five years of the licence — are limited to 0.2 promille, less than a single drink. The 0.5 limit applies only after those five years.

questions.q: A driver has held their licence for six years. What is their legal alcohol limit?
questions.e: After the first five licence years the standard limit of 0.5 promille applies. (The wise answer remains: if you drive, don't drink.)

questions.q: Your medicine box carries a yellow warning sticker. What does it mean?
a: The medicine is out of date
It can affect your driving — check before you drive
You must take it before driving
questions.e: The yellow sticker marks medicines that can impair reaction time. It means: ask the pharmacist or read the leaflet before driving — with some of these, driving is forbidden.

questions.q: How much cannabis or cocaine may legally be in your blood while driving?
a: None — any measurable amount is an offence
questions.e: For illegal drugs the law is zero tolerance, checked by roadside saliva test. There is no 'small enough' the way there is with alcohol.

questions.q: You are stationary at a red light, engine running, and answer a text with the phone in your hand. Offence?
a: No — the car is not moving
Yes — waiting at a light still counts as driving
Only if the police see it
questions.e: The ban is on holding a mobile device while driving — and standing in traffic is still driving. In a cradle, operated hands-free, it would be legal.

questions.q: Which insurance is legally required for every car on the public road?
questions.e: WA (wettelijke aansprakelijkheid) covers the damage you do to others and is mandatory. All-risk cover for your own car is optional.

questions.q: A seven-year-old child of 1.20 m sits in the back wearing only the normal seatbelt. Who is committing an offence?
a: The driver — the child needs a child seat
questions.e: Under 1.35 m a child needs an approved child seat or booster; the belt alone is not lawful. For passengers under 12 the responsibility — and the fine — is the driver's.

questions.q: Under this sign, may you stop briefly to let a passenger out?
a: Yes — it forbids parking, not stopping
No — you may not even halt
questions.e: The single slash (E1) forbids parking only. Stopping — briefly letting passengers in or out, or loading — is legally a different act and remains allowed.

questions.q: Under this sign, may you halt for ten seconds to drop someone off?
a: No — this sign forbids even stopping
questions.e: The X (E2) is the stopping ban — the total ban. If you may not even stop, you certainly may not park or drop off.

questions.q: You find a parking gap three metres from the corner of a junction. No signs anywhere. May you park?
a: Yes — no sign means no ban
No — within 5 metres of a junction parking is automatically forbidden
questions.e: The most important parking bans are never signed. Within five metres of a junction parking is forbidden by law — sightlines are everyone's safety.

questions.q: You park inside this zone at 13:15 and walk away without doing anything else. Legal?
a: No — you must display a parking disc set to 13:30
questions.e: In a parkeerschijfzone you must display a parking disc set to your arrival time rounded UP to the next half hour — then you may stay the posted maximum.

questions.q: Evening mist, visibility about 200 metres. May you switch on the rear fog light?
questions.e: The rear fog light is legal only when visibility drops below 50 metres. Above that it dazzles the driver behind and masks your brake lights — an offence.

questions.q: What is the legal minimum tread depth for car tyres?
questions.e: 1.6 millimetres. Below that the tyre is illegal — and in rain genuinely dangerous, because tread is what channels water away.

questions.q: Which driving habit saves fuel?
a: Staying in low gear at high revs for control
questions.e: Low revs in a high gear is the efficient place to be. On eco questions the calm answer — early upshifts, steady speed, anticipation — is always the right one.

questions.q: A ball bounces into the road from between parked cars, thirty metres ahead. The road is otherwise clear. What do you do?
a: Brake firmly — a child may follow
questions.e: A ball never crosses alone. Treat it as a child already stepping out: brake hard now. Swerving around the ball answers the wrong hazard.

questions.q: Dusk and drizzle outside the built-up area, limit 80. One question asks if you MAY drive 80, another if it is WISE. What is the correct pair of answers?
questions.e: 'May you' asks about the law — 80 is legal here. 'Is it wise' asks about safety — in dusk and rain it is not. The exam plants exactly this pair; answer the verb that was asked.
